newsitem.title: USA: U.S. calls on Israel to free up Palestinian funds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls on Israel to free up Palestinian funds.

text.p: Israel's decision to withhold $70 million worth of funds owed to the Palestinian Authority is counter-productive and should be reversed, the State Department said on Tuesday.

"We have told the Israeli government ... that we believe that that measure is counter-productive and while we do understand that security is the number one priority at this moment ... we believe it's counter-productive to withhold these funds," State Department spokesman James Foley said.
"It would be helpful if it was rescinded," he told reporters.

Following last week's double suicide bombing that killed 13 people at a Jerusalem market, Israel's Treasury said on Monday it had frozen the transfer of $70 million in VAT and customs duties it owes the Palestinian Authority under a 1994 economic protocol, until the Authority steps up its war against anti-Israel violence.

The move will deepen the Palestinian Authority's financial crisis and make it difficult to cover operating costs and pay public sector salaries. Israel transferred some 1.2 billion shekels ($339 million) to the Palestinian Authority in 1996. The Authority's official 1997 budget stands at $866 million.

Foley said the Israeli move could hinder joint Israeli and Palestinian interests, as well as "the economic well-being of Palestinians and building the kind of trust and confidence which is vital to restarting the negotiations."

High-level peace talks stopped in March, but Israel and the PLO agreed last week that joint committees would renew talks on outstanding issues such as the opening of Gaza air and sea ports and safe passage between the West Bank and Gaza.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is engaged in telephone diplomacy with leaders in the region, Foley said.
In a call to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Monday, Albright stressed the need to address security challenges in the region, Foley said.

Albright also planned to speak with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and has already spoken to Jordan's King Hussein, Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, Foley said.
In addition, Albright was to make a speech on the Middle East on Wednesday at the National Press Club in Washington.
Albright plans to travel to the Middle East soon, but not until special U.S. envoy Dennis Ross returns from a trip to the region set to begin at the end of this week, Foley said.

"She's planning to go soon, she's made that determination," Foley said. "She will obviously await the results of Ross's trip. Those results will obviously help to inform her own preparations for her trip."
